read.sections.0.heading.source: How a camera matches a face

read.sections.0.text.source: Facial recognition is a kind of AI that tries to tell who a person is from their face. First, the software finds a face in a photo or a video. Then it measures the face, such as the distance between the eyes. It turns these measurements into a set of numbers called a template. Next, it compares that template with others and gives a score for how alike they are. A phone that opens for your face checks one face against one template, its owner's. It usually keeps only the template, not a photo. A search compares one face with many faces in a database. Either way, a match is the software's best guess, not proof of who someone is.
read.sections.0.text.back: Facial recognition is a kind of AI that tries to tell who a person is from their face. First the software finds a face in a photo or video. Then it measures the face, such as the distance between the eyes, and turns the measurements into a set of numbers called a template. Next it compares that template with other templates and gives a score for how alike they are. A phone that unlocks with your face checks one face against one template, the owner's. Usually the phone keeps only the template, not a photo. A search compares one face with many faces in a database. Either way, a match is only the software's best guess, not proof of who someone is.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Facial recognition is AI that tries to name a person from their face. First, it finds a face in a photo. Then it measures the face, like how far apart the eyes are. It turns this into numbers, called a template. Next, it compares templates. It scores how alike they are. A phone checks one face against its owner's template. It usually keeps the template, not a photo. A search checks one face against many in a database. A match is a guess, not proof.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Facial recognition is AI that tries to tell a person's name from their face. First it finds a face in a photo. Then it measures the face, such as how far apart the eyes are. It turns this into numbers called a template. Next it compares templates. It gives a score for how alike they are. A phone checks one face against the owner's template. Usually it keeps the template, not a photo. A search checks one face against many faces in a database. A match is a guess, not proof.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Where it is used, and what can go wrong
read.sections.1.heading.back: Where it is used, and what can go wrong

read.sections.1.text.source: Face scans now open phones. At some airports, they replace showing a passport. At Singapore's Changi Airport, many travellers now pass the passport check by having their face and eyes scanned. But mistakes can be serious. In 2019, a science agency of the United States government tested 189 face recognition tools. Many of them wrongly matched two different people more often for some groups. These included women, older people, children and people of some backgrounds. The best tools made far fewer mistakes. A wrong match in a police search could get someone blamed for something they did not do. Cameras in public places could also pick out people in a crowd without them knowing. That is a risk to privacy.
read.sections.1.text.back: Today face scans are used to unlock phones. In some airports face scans are used instead of showing a passport. At Singapore's Changi Airport many travellers pass passport control by scanning their face and eyes. But mistakes can be serious. In 2019 a US government science agency tested 189 facial recognition tools. Many matched two different people as the same person more often in some groups, including women, older people, children and people of certain backgrounds. The best tools made far fewer mistakes. An incorrect match in a police search could get someone accused of something they did not do. Cameras in public places could also pick out people in a crowd without them knowing. That is a risk to privacy.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Face scans open phones. At some airports, they take the place of a passport. At Changi Airport in Singapore, many people scan their face and eyes. read.sections.1.simpler.back: Face scans are used to unlock phones. In some airports they are used instead of a passport. At Changi Airport in Singapore many people scan their face and eyes. read.sections.2.text.source: Because of these risks, places have made different choices. In 2019, San Francisco became the first US city to stop its police and other city offices from using face recognition. A European Union law has banned some uses since February 2025. Police there may not use live face recognition in public places. A few serious cases are allowed, such as a search for a missing person. A judge or another official who does not work for the police must agree first. The law also bans building face databases by copying face photos in bulk from the internet or from security cameras. Uses that are not banned must still follow other laws. For example, the EU's privacy law protects face data. Singapore, by contrast, chose to use face scans at its airport.
read.sections.2.text.back: Because of these risks, places choose differently. In 2019 San Francisco became the first US city to ban the police and other city offices from using facial recognition. European Union law has banned some uses since February 2025. Police there may not use live facial recognition in public places, but it is allowed in a few serious cases, such as searching for a missing person, if a judge or another official who does not work for the police approves first. The law also bans building face databases by copying large numbers of face pictures from the internet or security cameras. Uses that are not banned still have to follow other laws; for example, EU privacy law protects face data. Singapore, by contrast, chose to use face scanning at the airport.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Places make different choices. In 2019, San Francisco stopped its police from using face scans. Other city offices had to stop too. A judge or an official must say yes first. It also bans copying lots of face photos for a face database. Privacy laws still cover other uses. Singapore chose to use face scans at its airport.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Places choose differently. In 2019 San Francisco banned the police from using face scanning. Other city offices had to stop too. watch.summary.source: In this video, a reporter talks with an expert in computer vision who is also a lawyer. Facial recognition is used to open phones, name friends in photos and help people board planes. It works by finding patterns in faces. To learn them, it needs many photos, sometimes millions, with labels that say who is in them. Police see a benefit. They can search many photos quickly, and that matters in serious cases. But the expert names two kinds of worry. If the tool is wrong, it may name the wrong person. Research found it works worse for some groups. If the tool is right, people could be watched and tracked without knowing. Some cities in the United States, such as San Francisco, banned government use. The expert says people should decide together how it is used.
watch.summary.back: In this video a journalist talks with a computer vision expert who is also a lawyer. Facial recognition is used to unlock phones, name friends in photos and help people board planes. It works by finding patterns in faces. To learn these patterns it needs many photos, sometimes millions, with labels saying who is in them. Police see benefits: they can search many photos quickly, which matters in serious cases. But the expert talks about two kinds of worry. If the tool answers wrongly, it may name the wrong person; research found it works worse for some groups. If the tool answers correctly, people may be watched and tracked without knowing. Some US cities, such as San Francisco, ban the government from using it. The expert says people should decide together how to use it.

educatorNotes.0.source: The real facts, simplified (claims/DW12.md). NIST (December 2019) tested 189 mostly commercial algorithms from 99 developers: false matches often 10 to over 100 times more frequent for some groups, varying by algorithm; higher in women than men, in the elderly and in children, and highest for West and East African and East Asian faces in one test (some algorithms developed in China reversed this); the most accurate algorithms showed far fewer errors. Phones: Apple's security guide says Face ID saves mathematical representations of the face, not images, and they never leave the device; other phones differ. Singapore (ICA, 24 October 2024): passport-less clearance with face and iris at all four Changi terminals since 30 September 2024, for residents on arrival and departure and visitors on departure; average clearance time down from 25 to 10 seconds; travellers should still carry passports. San Francisco (May 2019): city personnel, including police, may not buy or use facial recognition; airports and other federally regulated places were not included. EU AI Act, Article 5, in force since 2 February 2025: police use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces is banned except where strictly necessary to search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation or for missing persons, to prevent a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack, or to find suspects of listed serious crimes; each use needs prior authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority (in an emergency, asked for within 24 hours), and only where national law allows it. The scraping ban covers building or expanding facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV. Uses the AI Act doesn't ban still fall under other laws: the GDPR treats biometric data used to identify someone as sensitive data, generally not to be processed without, for example, explicit consent or a law with safeguards; identifying people later from recordings is high-risk under the AI Act, with duties due from 2 December 2027 after the 2026 AI Omnibus. Rules change: check them before teaching.
educatorNotes.0.back: The facts in brief (claims/DW12.md). NIST (December 2019) tested 189 algorithms, mostly commercial, from 99 developers, and found false matches in some groups were often 10 to more than 100 times more frequent, varying by algorithm: higher for women than men, for older people and for children, and in one test highest for West African, East African and East Asian faces (some algorithms developed in China showed the reverse). The most accurate algorithms had far fewer errors. Phones: Apple's security guide says Face ID stores face data as a mathematical representation, not an image, and the data never leaves the device; other phones may differ. Singapore (ICA, 24 October 2024): passport-free clearance by face and iris at all four Changi terminals from 30 September 2024, for residents arriving and leaving and visitors leaving; average clearance time fell from 25 seconds to 10. Travellers should still carry passports. San Francisco (May 2019): city staff, including police, may not buy or use facial recognition; the airport and other places under federal oversight are excluded. The EU AI Act, Article 5, in force from 2 February 2025: police may not use real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces except when strictly necessary to search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation, or missing persons; to prevent a specific, serious and imminent threat to life or terrorism; or to locate suspects of listed serious crimes. Each use needs prior authorisation from a judicial or independent administrative authority (in emergencies, within 24 hours) and is possible only where national law allows. The scraping ban covers building or expanding facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV. Uses the AI Act does not ban still fall under other laws: the GDPR treats biometric data used to identify people as sensitive, generally banning processing without, for example, explicit consent or a law with safeguards. Retrospective identification from recorded images is high-risk under the AI Act, with obligations from 2 December 2027 after the 2026 AI Omnibus. Laws can change; check before teaching.

educatorNotes.1.source: Discussion tips for Speak: accept yes, no or yes with rules when the learner gives a reason; useful prompts are who decides (a judge, the police, a city council), for how long data is kept, and what happens after a wrong match. Lesson 8 (why tools can work worse for some groups) and Lesson 16 (who makes the rules for AI) are good links.
educatorNotes.1.back: Tips for the Speak discussion: accept yes, no or yes-with-rules when learners give reasons. Useful prompts: who decides (a judge, police or a city council), how long data is kept, and what happens after an incorrect match. Lesson 8 (why tools work worse for some groups) and Lesson 16 (who sets rules for AI) connect well.
